sub: The heart of the Syro-Malankara Church: what it is, how it unfolds, and how to take part
sec: What the word means

“Qurbono” is the West Syriac form of the Syriac word qurbānā (in the East Syriac pronunciation, Qurbana). It comes from the root q-r-b, “to draw near” and “to offer”. The Holy Qurbono is the offering by which Christ draws near to us and we are drawn near to the Father.

It is not simply a prayer meeting or a devotion. It is the Eucharistic sacrifice: the one sacrifice of Christ on the Cross made present, in which bread and wine become truly, really and substantially his Body and Blood, and are given to us as food for eternal life.
Its roots

The Syro-Malankara Church celebrates the Holy Qurbono in the West Syriac (Antiochene) tradition, the liturgy of the ancient Church of Antioch and Jerusalem. Its principal anaphora (Eucharistic prayer) bears the name of St James, “the brother of the Lord” and first bishop of Jerusalem; the Church also uses other approved anaphoras.

When Archbishop Mar Ivanios entered full communion with the Catholic Church in 1930, this liturgy was kept whole. The Catholic Church treasures it: the Eastern Churches are of equal dignity with the Latin Church and are asked to preserve their own rites (Orientalium Ecclesiarum 3, 6).
How it unfolds

1. Preparation. Before the public celebration the priest prepares the altar, the bread and the wine (mixed with a little water), with prayers of humility. The bread is leavened, as in the Syriac tradition.

2. The opening and the Word. The veil of the sanctuary is opened and the celebration begins with incense and hymns. The Trisagion (“Holy are you, O God…”) is sung. Readings from the Apostles are proclaimed, then the Gospel (Evangelion), heard standing. The Sedro, a long prayer with incense, asks forgiveness and blessing. The Nicene Creed is professed.

3. The Anaphora. The peace (Shlomo) is passed from the altar through the people: we are reconciled before we offer. The priest invites: “Let our minds, our thoughts and our hearts be on high”, and all sing the Sanctus. He recalls the Last Supper and repeats Christ's words over the bread and the cup. Then comes the Epiclesis: the Holy Spirit is called down upon the gifts and upon the people, and the people answer “Kurielaison” three times. In the great intercessions (Thubden) the Church remembers the living and the dead, the Mother of God, the saints and the fathers.

4. Communion. The Lord's Prayer is said. The priest breaks the Holy Body and unites it with the Blood. He lifts the Mysteries: “Holy things for the holy.” The faithful receive the Body dipped in the Blood (intinction). After communion come thanksgiving, the final blessing and the dismissal; the priest bids farewell to the altar with a moving prayer that he may return to it in peace.
What the Church believes
It is a true sacrifice: not a new sacrifice, but the one sacrifice of the Cross made present, so that its fruits are applied to us (CCC 1366–1367).

Christ is truly present under the appearances of bread and wine, whole and entire, Body and Blood, soul and divinity; this change the Church calls transubstantiation (CCC 1374–1376; Council of Trent).
The Holy Spirit makes the gifts holy. Eastern liturgies give great emphasis to the Epiclesis, the invocation of the Spirit (CCC 1353).
It is the action of the whole Church, Head and members, on earth and in heaven, united with the Pope and the bishops, whose names are remembered at the altar.
How to take part well

Come before it begins; the prayers of the beginning belong to you too. Stand when the Church stands; it is the posture of the risen. Answer aloud and sing. Follow the actions: incense, veil, peace, elevation; each speaks.
Receive Holy Communion with faith and reverence, having kept the Eucharistic fast laid down by the Church. After the Qurbono, stay for the thanksgiving; then live what you received.
The sanctuary and its signs

In a Syro-Malankara church the sanctuary (Madbaho) is raised and separated from the nave by a curtain. The curtain is opened and closed at fixed moments: closed during the preparation, opened at the beginning of the public celebration, closed again at moments of great mystery. It teaches that the Holy Qurbono is the opening of heaven to us, and that we approach it with awe.

On the altar lies the tablitho, a consecrated board on which the Mysteries are celebrated. Liturgical fans with small bells (marvahtho), shaped like the wings of the seraphim, are waved over the gifts, recalling the angels who surround the throne of God (Isaiah 6:2). The censer, with its little bells, is used often: the incense rises like prayer (Psalm 141:2).
Vestments and gestures

The priest wears the kuthino (white tunic), the hamnikho (stole), the zenoro (girdle), the zendo (cuffs) and the phayno (the large outer vestment, like a cope). The deacon wears an orarion over the shoulder. Each vestment is put on with a prayer.

The people make the sign of the Cross often, bow at the Trisagion and at the blessing, answer “Kurielaison” and sing the hymns. At the peace, the peace passes hand to hand from the altar through the whole congregation: Christ's peace comes from the altar, not from ourselves.
Questions people ask

Why is the curtain drawn? Not to hide the Mysteries from the people, but to express their holiness. Moses removed his sandals before the burning bush (Exodus 3:5); the curtain teaches the same reverence.
Why are the prayers sung? The West Syriac tradition believes that the Church on earth joins the song of the angels. Singing makes the prayer the prayer of all.
Why Communion by intinction? The Holy Body is dipped in the Holy Blood and given with a spoon or by the priest's hand, so that the faithful receive the Lord under both kinds.
How often may I receive? Every day if properly disposed; a second time on the same day only within a Holy Qurbono in which you take part.
notes: Anyone conscious of grave (mortal) sin must receive the sacrament of Confession before receiving Holy Communion (CCC 1385; 1 Corinthians 11:27–29).
Participation in the Holy Qurbono on Sundays and holy days of obligation is a grave duty of every Catholic, unless excused for a serious reason such as illness or the care of infants (CCC 2180–2181).
Catholics should receive Communion only in Catholic celebrations, except in the specific cases foreseen by Church law (CCC 1398–1401).
The liturgy belongs to the Church, not to any individual: no priest or community may add, remove or change anything on its own authority (Sacrosanctum Concilium 22).
Treat the consecrated Body and Blood with the utmost care; no particle should fall or be left behind.
The Eucharistic fast before Holy Communion is laid down by the particular law of each Church sui iuris; follow the current norm of the Syro-Malankara Church (CCEO c. 713 §2).

sub: How the Syro-Malankara Church walks through the mystery of Christ in seven seasons, from the Sanctification of the Church to the Holy Cross
sec: Why a liturgical year?

Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever (Hebrews 13:8), yet in the course of a year the Church unfolds his whole mystery, from the announcement of his birth to his coming again, so that we may enter it step by step and be transformed (CCC 1163–1171).

The West Syriac tradition, which the Syro-Malankara Church received from Antioch, sings the year more than it explains it. Its hymns (madrashe and qolo) for each Sunday lead the faithful through the events of salvation, so that each season becomes a school of prayer.
Sunday and the date of Qyomtho

Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, is the foundation and heart of the whole year. Each Sunday has its own readings, usually from the Old Testament, the Acts or Catholic Epistles, St Paul and the Gospel, and its own hymns.

The most important feast is Qyomtho (Easter). Its date follows the rule of the Council of Nicaea: the Sunday after the first full moon after the spring equinox. Many other days depend on it: the Nineveh fast, the Great Fast, Sulokho (the Ascension, on the fortieth day) and Pentecost (the fiftieth day). Because the date of Qyomtho moves, the number of Sundays after Denho and after Pentecost changes from year to year.
1. Suboro: the season of announcements

The year begins with two Sundays that look at the Church herself: Qudos Eetho, the Sanctification of the Church, and Hudos Eetho, the Dedication of the Church. Before celebrating the coming of Christ, the Church remembers what she is: the holy dwelling of God among his people.

Then come the Sundays of the announcements, which follow the Gospel of Luke and Matthew: the annunciation to Zechariah, the annunciation to Mary, the visitation of Mary to Elizabeth, the birth of John the Baptist, the revelation to Joseph, and the Sunday before Yaldo with the genealogy of the Lord. The Twenty-Five Days' Fast (1–25 December) accompanies these weeks.
2. Yaldo and Denho: the birth and manifestation of the Lord

Yaldo, the Birth of the Lord (25 December), opens the season of the Nativity. The Sundays after Yaldo remember the flight into Egypt and the childhood of Christ; on 1 January the Church keeps the Naming and Circumcision of the Lord.

Denho (6 January) celebrates the Baptism of the Lord in the Jordan and the manifestation of the Holy Trinity. Its liturgy includes the solemn blessing of water. The Sundays after Denho remember the witness of John the Baptist and the beginning of the Lord's ministry; before the Great Fast come the Sunday of the Priests (Kohne) and the Sunday of the Faithful Departed (Aneede). Mayaltho, the Presentation of the Lord in the Temple, is kept on 2 February. The Three Days' (Nineveh) Fast is kept in the weeks before the Great Fast.
3. The Great Fast and the week of the Passion

The Great Fast begins on Shubkono, the Monday of reconciliation, when the faithful ask forgiveness of one another before entering the fast. The Sunday before it is Kothine, the wedding at Cana: Christ who changed water into wine will change us.

The Sundays of the fast are named after the healings of the Lord: Garbo (the leper), Mshario (the paralytic), Knanoitho (the Canaanite woman), Kpiphtho (the bent woman) and Samio (the blind man). The middle of the fast is marked on its Wednesday; the fortieth Friday closes the forty days, followed by the Saturday of Lazarus.

Hosanna Sunday opens the week of the Passion. On Pesaha Thursday the Church celebrates the Last Supper with the washing of the feet; on Good Friday the long service of the Passion, with the veneration and burial of the Cross; on Holy Saturday the Church keeps vigil at the tomb. The period from the beginning of the Great Fast to the first Sunday after Pentecost is called the Season of the Passover.
4–7. Qyomtho, Pentecost, Transfiguration and the Holy Cross

4. Qyomtho. The Resurrection is the feast of feasts, celebrated in the night with the proclamation of the risen Lord and the service of peace. The New Sunday follows, with the Gospel of St Thomas; Sulokho, the Ascension, is kept on the fortieth day.

5. Pentecost. The coming of the Holy Spirit is celebrated with the special prayers of kneeling, in which the Church asks the Spirit to come upon her as upon the apostles. The Sundays after Pentecost show the life of the Church in the Spirit; Sts Peter and Paul (29 June) and the Dukrono of St Thomas (3 July) fall in this season, and on 15 July the Church remembers Mar Ivanios.

6. Transfiguration (M'thale, 6 August). Christ's glory on the mountain gives hope in suffering. The Shunoyo, the falling asleep and assumption of Mary (15 August), and her Nativity (8 September) fall in this season.

7. Sleebo (the Holy Cross, 14 September). The last season of the year looks at the Cross and at the end of time: the sign of the Son of Man, the judgment and the Second Coming of Christ. The Reunion Day (20 September) recalls the entry of Mar Ivanios and his companions into full communion with the Catholic Church in 1930.
The great feasts

Feasts of the Lord: Yaldo, Denho, Mayaltho (2 February), Qyomtho, Sulokho, Pentecost and M'thale. Observed like feasts of the Lord: Suboro (the Annunciation, 25 March), Sts Peter and Paul (29 June), the Dukrono of St Thomas (3 July), the Shunoyo (15 August) and the Holy Cross (14 September).
On these days, and on every Sunday, the faithful take part in the Holy Qurbono, refrain from servile work and keep the day holy with Scripture, prayer and good works.
Fasts (Nombu)
Canonical fasts: the Twenty-Five Days' Fast (1–25 December), the Three Days' (Nineveh) Fast, and the Fifty Days' Great Fast.

Pious fasts, recommended though not binding by law: the Thirteen Days' Fast of the Apostles (before 29 June), the Fifteen Days' Fast before the Shunoyo (1–15 August) and the Eight Days' Fast before the Nativity of Mary (1–8 September). Many also keep the Mar Ivanios fast (1–15 July) for the cause of the Servant of God.
In the Syriac tradition fasting is joined to prayer at the canonical hours, to reconciliation and to almsgiving. A fast that leaves the heart hard has missed its purpose (Isaiah 58:6–7).
Living the year at home

Learn the name of each Sunday and read its Gospel at home on Saturday evening. Keep the fasts as a family, with simpler meals and gifts to the poor. Ask forgiveness of one another on Shubkono; keep silence and prayer on Good Friday; greet one another with the joy of the Resurrection at Qyomtho.
Teach children the meaning of the great feasts and of the saints of our Church. When the rhythm of the Church enters the home, the family becomes a little church.
notes: On all Fridays and on the days of the Twenty-Five Days', Three Days' and Great Fasts, the faithful abstain from meat. The days between the Nineveh fast and the Great Fast, and the fifty days from Qyomtho to Pentecost, are exempt.

On the days of the Nineveh fast, on Shubkono and on the Fridays of the Great Fast, and from the fortieth Friday to Qyomtho, the faithful also abstain from fish and eggs; on Good Friday also from milk and milk products. There is no abstinence on the closing day of a fast.
All are obliged to take part in the special services of Good Friday; on Maundy Thursday all, young and old, should take part in the Holy Qurbono and receive worthily.
Those who are sick, pregnant or nursing, the elderly and those doing heavy work should consult their pastor; fasting must never endanger health (cf. CCC 2043).
These rules follow the Syro-Malankara Sacred Lectionary; always follow the current circular of your eparchy.

The Syro-Malankara Church uses the liturgy of St James in the West Syriac tradition; its calendar and hymns differ from the East Syriac (Syro-Malabar) and Roman calendars, though the great feasts are shared.

sub: Why we confess, how to examine our conscience, how to make a good confession, and what the Church asks of us
sec: Christ gave this sacrament

On the evening of Easter the risen Lord breathed on the apostles and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:22–23). Through the bishops and priests, their successors, Christ continues to forgive sins in the Church (CCC 1441–1445).

This sacrament has many names: conversion, penance, confession, forgiveness and reconciliation (CCC 1423–1424). In Kerala we usually say “Kumbasaram”. It is the sacrament of the prodigal son coming home and of the Father who runs to embrace him (Luke 15:20).
Why confess to a priest?

Only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7). But God chose to forgive through his Church: Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive and to retain, which they could not use without hearing the sins (CCC 1461–1462). The priest is not a judge who condemns but a minister of mercy who acts in the person of Christ, the Good Shepherd seeking the lost sheep (CCC 1465).

Sin is never purely private. It wounds the Body of Christ, the Church. So reconciliation with God is also reconciliation with the Church (CCC 1445, 1469). Hearing the words of absolution spoken aloud gives a certainty of forgiveness that our feelings alone cannot give.
Mortal and venial sin

Mortal sin destroys charity in the heart: it is a sin whose object is grave matter, committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857). Grave matter is specified by the Ten Commandments. Mortal sin, unless repented and forgiven, separates us from God for ever (CCC 1861).

Venial sin weakens charity but does not destroy it (CCC 1862–1863). Confessing everyday faults is strongly recommended: it helps us form our conscience, fight evil tendencies, let ourselves be healed by Christ and grow in the life of the Spirit (CCC 1458).
Examining the conscience

An honest examination is the first step. Some questions, following the Commandments: Do I pray daily? Have I denied my faith or been ashamed of it? Have I used God's name carelessly or sworn falsely? Have I missed the Holy Qurbana or Mass on Sundays and days of obligation without serious reason?

Have I honored my parents and cared for them? Have I been unjust, violent or harsh at home, at work, with servants or employees? Have I harmed life: by anger, hatred, abortion, abuse of alcohol or drugs, reckless driving? Have I sinned against chastity in thought, word or deed, alone or with others, through pornography? Have I been faithful in marriage?

Have I stolen, cheated, taken bribes, failed to pay just wages or debts, wasted money while others are in need? Have I lied, gossiped, ruined another's good name, posted harmful things on social media? Have I been envious, greedy, proud, lazy in my duties? Have I neglected the poor?

Children and young people can ask more simply: Did I pray? Did I obey my parents and teachers? Did I tell lies, fight, use bad words, take what is not mine, cheat in exams, waste time on the phone, hurt anyone?
The three acts of the penitent

1. Contrition: sorrow of soul and hatred for the sin committed, with the resolution not to sin again. Perfect contrition comes from love of God; imperfect contrition (attrition) comes from fear of punishment or the ugliness of sin, and is sufficient for the sacrament (CCC 1451–1453).

2. Confession: telling the priest all mortal sins of which, after careful examination, we are conscious, with their kind and number, as far as we can (CCC 1456). Speak simply and honestly; there is no need for long stories or for naming other people.

3. Satisfaction: doing the penance the priest gives, to repair the harm and restore our habits as disciples of Christ (CCC 1459–1460). Where we have harmed others, we must also make it right: return what was taken, restore a damaged reputation, ask forgiveness.
How to make a good confession
Before: pray to the Holy Spirit for light; examine your conscience; awaken sorrow by looking at the crucifix and remembering God's love.

In the confessional: make the sign of the Cross; say how long it has been since your last confession and, if helpful, your state of life (married, student, priest or religious); confess your sins; listen to the priest's counsel and accept the penance; pray an act of contrition; receive absolution with faith. In the Eastern Churches the prayer of absolution often asks God to forgive the penitent; in the Latin Church the priest says “I absolve you”. Both are true and valid forms of the same sacrament.

A traditional act of contrition: O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended you, and I detest all my sins because of your just punishments, but most of all because they offend you, my God, who are all good and deserving of all my love. I firmly resolve, with the help of your grace, to sin no more and to avoid the near occasion of sin. Amen. (Any approved act of contrition may be used, such as the one taught in your parish catechism.)
After: thank God; do the penance soon; repair any harm done; avoid the occasions of sin; come back regularly, not only when burdened by grave sin.
What the sacrament gives

Reconciliation with God, by which grace is restored; reconciliation with the Church; remission of the eternal punishment due to mortal sin and, at least in part, of temporal punishment; peace and serenity of conscience and spiritual consolation; and an increase of strength for the Christian battle (CCC 1468–1470, 1496).

Many people find that the hardest step is the first one, the walk to the confessional. Beyond it is the joy of the Father: “this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found” (Luke 15:24).
Children, first confession and frequent confession

Children who have reached the age of discretion (around seven) are prepared for their first confession before their first Holy Communion (CCC 1457; c. 914). Parents should go with them and confess themselves; children learn most from what they see.

The saints recommend confessing regularly, for example monthly, and before the great feasts. Many parishes offer confession during the Twenty-Five Days' Fast and the Great Fast or Lent; make use of these times.
notes: Every Catholic who has reached the age of discretion must confess grave sins at least once a year (CCC 2042, 1457).

One who is conscious of mortal sin must not receive Holy Communion without first going to confession, except when there is a grave reason and no opportunity to confess; then an act of perfect contrition must be made, with the intention of confessing as soon as possible (CCC 1457, 1385).

Deliberately hiding a mortal sin in confession makes the confession invalid and adds the sin of sacrilege; the hidden sin and the sacrilege must be confessed. Forgetting a sin is not hiding it: the forgotten sin is forgiven and should be mentioned at the next confession.
The priest is bound by the absolute seal of confession: he may never reveal or use what he hears, under the most severe penalties (CCC 1467; Code of Canon Law c. 983; CCEO c. 733).
Absolution requires real contrition and the purpose of amendment; it cannot be given to one who refuses to give up a grave sin or to repair a grave injustice.

General absolution without individual confession is allowed only in grave necessity (danger of death, or very large numbers with no possibility of individual confession for a long time); grave sins must then be confessed individually as soon as possible (CCC 1483).
Some very grave sins carry penalties whose remission is reserved; if this concerns you, speak to a priest, who will explain the path of reconciliation.

sub: Mamodeeso and Holy Myron: how we are born into Christ and sealed with the Spirit
sec: Christ commands it

Before his Ascension the risen Lord sent the apostles: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). On the day of Pentecost Peter told the crowd: “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ so that your sins may be forgiven; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).

Baptism is the door of the Christian life and of the other sacraments (CCC 1213). It is called the bath of new birth (Titus 3:5) and enlightenment (Hebrews 6:4): “no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit” (John 3:5).
How it is celebrated in our Church

In the Syro-Malankara Church, following the West Syriac tradition of Antioch, Baptism and Chrismation with Holy Myron are celebrated together. The priest is the ordinary minister, using the Myron consecrated by the Major Archbishop-Catholicos.

The rite has two parts. First, the reception of the catechumen: prayers of exorcism; the renunciation of Satan, facing west, the place of darkness; the profession of faith, facing east, towards Christ the rising Sun; the anointing with the oil of catechumens on the forehead.

Then the Baptism: the solemn blessing of the water, with the Holy Spirit called down upon it and the holy Myron poured into it in the form of a cross; the Baptism itself, with the words “N. is baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit”; the anointing of the whole body with Holy Myron, the seal of the Holy Spirit; the clothing in white and, in the tradition, the crowning of the newly baptized as a sign of the royal dignity of the children of God.
What Baptism does

Baptism forgives original sin and all personal sins, with all punishment due to sin (CCC 1263). It makes us a new creation, adopted children of God, members of Christ and temples of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1265). It joins us to the Church, the Body of Christ (CCC 1267).

It marks the soul with an indelible spiritual seal, which no sin can erase; therefore Baptism is never repeated (CCC 1272). The weakness left by original sin remains, and the struggle against sin continues; but the baptized are never alone in that struggle.
The seal of the Spirit

Baptism, Chrismation (Confirmation) and the Holy Eucharist together are the sacraments of Christian initiation (CCC 1212). Chrismation completes baptismal grace: the baptized are anointed with Holy Myron (Chrism), consecrated by the bishop, and receive the Holy Spirit as the apostles did at Pentecost, to be strong witnesses of Christ (CCC 1285, 1303).
Like Baptism, Chrismation marks the soul with an indelible character and is received only once (CCC 1304).
Parents and godparents

Children are baptized in the faith of the Church, and parents promise to raise them in that faith (CCC 1250–1253). Godparents (sponsors) must be practicing Catholics who have received the sacraments of initiation, chosen to help the child live as a Christian. They are not chosen only for family honor.
Choosing a Christian name, often the name of a saint, gives the child a heavenly friend and a model (CCC 2156).
In danger of death

In an emergency anyone, even a non-baptized person, can baptize, if he or she intends to do what the Church does: pour water on the head of the person, saying, “N., I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1256). Inform the parish priest afterwards, so that it can be recorded and the other rites completed.

Those who die for the faith before being baptized (baptism of blood), and catechumens who die with the explicit desire for Baptism, are saved without the sacrament (CCC 1258–1259). For children who die without Baptism, the Church entrusts them to the mercy of God and hopes for their salvation (CCC 1261).
Living our Baptism

Remember the date of your Baptism and celebrate it. Renew your baptismal promises at Easter. Teach children that the font is where they were born as Christians. Visit your baptismal church when you can.
The white garment and the lighted candle given at Baptism are a call: keep the garment clean and the light burning until the Lord comes (cf. Matthew 25:1–13).
notes: Parents should ask for the Baptism of their children within the first weeks after birth and prepare for it; delay without a just reason is not right (CCC 1250; CCEO c. 686; c. 867).
Baptism must be recorded in the parish register; the baptismal certificate is needed for later sacraments, especially marriage.
A godparent must be at least sixteen years old (unless the bishop decides otherwise), confirmed, living a life of faith, and not the father or mother of the child (c. 874; CCEO c. 685).
Baptism validly given in other Christian Churches is not repeated when a person enters full communion with the Catholic Church.
In the Syro-Malankara Church Chrismation is given together with Baptism and is not postponed; the child has received both sacraments fully.
Children of Syro-Malankara parents belong to the Syro-Malankara Church even when baptized elsewhere; register the Baptism in your own parish and Church (CCEO c. 29).

sub: Kandeelo, the Service of the Lamp: Christ the physician of souls and bodies in the Syro-Malankara Church
sec: Christ the physician of souls and bodies

The Gospels are full of the sick who came to Jesus: the blind, the lepers, the paralyzed, the woman who touched the fringe of his cloak. He healed them as a sign that the Kingdom of God had come, and he sent the Twelve to do the same: they “anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them” (Mark 6:13).

The apostolic Church continued this ministry: “Are any among you sick? They should call for the elders of the church and have them pray over them, anointing them with oil in the name of the Lord. The prayer of faith will save the sick, and the Lord will raise them up; and anyone who has committed sins will be forgiven” (James 5:14–15; CCC 1510). The West Syriac prayers of this sacrament return again and again to one title of the Lord: the Physician of our souls and of our bodies, who heals the whole person.
Who should receive it

The Anointing of the Sick is not a sacrament only for the dying. It is for any of the faithful whose health is seriously endangered by sickness or old age: in a grave illness, before a serious operation, when the elderly become frail, or when a chronic illness grows worse (CCC 1514–1515; CCEO c. 737).

It may be repeated if the sick person recovers and then falls ill again, or if the same illness becomes more serious. Children who have reached the use of reason and are seriously ill may also receive it. Do not wait until the person is unconscious; call the priest while the sick person can still pray, make a confession and receive Holy Communion.
The name: Kandeelo, the Service of the Lamp

In the West Syriac tradition this sacrament is called the Kandeelo (Syriac qandilo, “lamp”), because the oil is blessed in a lamp and the service is celebrated around a lighted lamp. The lamp recalls the wise virgins who waited for the Bridegroom: “the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps” (Matthew 25:4). The sick Christian, too, keeps the lamp of faith burning while waiting for the Lord.

The oil recalls the Good Samaritan, who bandaged the wounds of the man left half dead, “having poured oil and wine on them” (Luke 10:34); the Fathers saw in the Samaritan Christ himself, who bends down to wounded humanity. St Ephrem loved to note that in Syriac the word for oil (meshho) and the name of the Anointed One (Mshiho) sound alike: the holy oil speaks of Christ, who comes to the sick in it.
The order of the service, step by step
1. Preparation. A small table is set with a clean cloth, a cross, the Gospel book, candles, incense and the lamp with olive oil. The priest vests and the family gathers around the sick person.

2. Opening and penitence. The service begins with the glory to the Holy Trinity, the Kauma (“Holy are you, O God… who was crucified for us, have mercy on us”) and Psalm 51, the great psalm of repentance. The Promiun and Sedro, prayed with incense, ask forgiveness of sins and healing for the servant of God.

3. Readings. Passages from the Apostle (above all James 5) and from the Gospel, recounting the healing works of Christ, are read. In the full traditional form the service is divided into several sections, each with its own prayers, readings and the lighting of a wick of the lamp.
4. The blessing of the oil. The priest prays over the oil, calling down the Holy Spirit so that it may become an oil of healing, of forgiveness and of protection against every evil.

5. The anointing. The priest anoints the sick person with the sign of the cross on the forehead and on other parts of the body, such as the hands, praying that God may heal him or her in body and soul and forgive every sin.

6. Conclusion. The Lord's Prayer is said; when possible the sick person receives Holy Communion; the priest blesses with the hand cross. The exact texts and their length follow the approved order (Taksa) of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church; in hospitals and in urgent cases a shorter form is used.
Many priests, one praying Church

James speaks of the “elders”, in the plural. For this reason the full Kandeelo was traditionally celebrated by several priests together, each reading a Gospel and praying over the oil, so that the sick person is surrounded by the prayer of the whole Church. In ordinary pastoral life one priest celebrates it, and the sacrament is complete.

The family and neighbors are not spectators. They answer the prayers, sing “Kurielaison”, hold the candles and pray for the sick person. In some parishes the sacrament is celebrated in church for the elderly and the sick together, on a chosen day, so that they experience the care of the community.
What the sacrament gives

The special grace of the Holy Spirit gives strength, peace and courage to bear the suffering of illness or old age; it unites the sick person to the Passion of Christ, so that suffering takes on a saving meaning; it forgives sins if the sick person could not make a confession; it restores bodily health if that is good for the salvation of the soul; and it prepares the person for the passage to eternal life (CCC 1520–1523).

The sick are not useless to the Church. By offering their pain with Christ they contribute to the good of the whole People of God (CCC 1522; Colossians 1:24). Many elderly members of our parishes carry the parish in prayer from their sickbeds.
Viaticum: food for the last journey

For those who are about to leave this life, the Church offers, besides Confession and the Anointing, Holy Communion as Viaticum, the “food for the journey” to the Father. Christ said: “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood have eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day” (John 6:54; CCC 1524–1525).

When death draws near, the family may keep a lamp burning, read the Gospel of the Passion or of the Resurrection, pray the Kauma and the prayers for the dying, and repeat short prayers to the sick person: “Lord Jesus, receive my soul.” Confession, Anointing and Viaticum together are the last sacraments of the Christian, given so that he or she may pass to the Father in peace.
How the family can help

Tell the parish priest early when someone is seriously ill, and do not hide the seriousness of the illness from the sick person out of misplaced kindness. Prepare the room: a table with a white cloth, a cross, a lamp or candles, a little cotton and a glass of water.

After the anointing, the cotton used to wipe the oil is not thrown away; by custom it is burned or buried reverently. Visit the sick, pray with them, read the Gospel to them, and help them to receive Confession and Holy Communion regularly. Caring for the sick is caring for Christ: “I was sick and you took care of me” (Matthew 25:36).
notes: Only a priest (and therefore a bishop) can validly administer the Anointing of the Sick; deacons and lay people cannot (CCC 1516; CCEO c. 739 §1).
Those who are conscious should, whenever possible, confess their sins before the Anointing; the Anointing forgives sins only when confession is impossible.

The sacrament is not given to the dead. If it is uncertain whether the person has died, the priest may give it conditionally; after certain death the Church prays for the departed with the prayers of the funeral.
Use only the oil blessed for this sacrament according to the law and books of our Church; what remains is not used for other purposes or thrown away, but absorbed in cotton and burned.

Eastern non-Catholic Christians (for example members of the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Churches) may receive the Anointing from a Catholic priest if they ask for it on their own and are rightly disposed; and when a Catholic minister cannot be reached, a Catholic may in necessity ask it of their priests (CCEO c. 671; Common Declaration of Pope John Paul II and Patriarch Ignatius Zakka I, 1984).
The Anointing is not a sign that the end has come and should not frighten the sick person; it is Christ's medicine for the time of weakness, and many recover after receiving it.

sub: The Crowning: the sacrament of married love in the West Syriac tradition of the Syro-Malankara Church
sec: God's plan from the beginning

“God created humankind in his image… male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). “Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Marriage is not a human invention; it is written into creation by God himself (CCC 1603).

Jesus restored marriage to its original dignity: “what God has joined together, let no one separate” (Mark 10:9). He worked his first sign at a wedding in Cana (John 2:1–11). For Christians marriage is a sacrament: the love of husband and wife becomes a sign of the love of Christ for his Church. St Paul writes: “This is a great mystery, and I am applying it to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32; CCC 1612–1617).
The marks of Christian marriage

Unity: one man and one woman, giving themselves to each other for life. Indissolubility: a valid sacramental marriage, once consummated, cannot be dissolved by any human power, only by death (CCC 1640, 2382). Fidelity: an exclusive love, without betrayal in body or heart. Openness to life: children are the supreme gift of marriage, and parents are the first teachers of the faith (CCC 1652–1653).

Free consent is the heart of marriage. No one may be forced to marry, whether by parents, by family pressure or by money; consent given under grave fear or deception can make a marriage invalid (CCC 1625–1628). Parents rightly guide and advise, as is the good custom of Kerala families, but the decision belongs to the two who will marry.
The blessing of the priest

In the Western Church the spouses are usually said to be the ministers of the sacrament. The Eastern tradition, which our Church shares, sees the priest who blesses the couple in the name of Christ as the one through whom Christ himself joins them; the priestly blessing is therefore required for validity (CCEO c. 828; CCC 1623). Both views agree that the free consent of the spouses is essential and that it is God who unites them.

For this reason the West Syriac marriage service is a service of blessing (burokho): it is above all a prayer, in which the Church asks the Holy Trinity to bless the couple as Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Rachel were blessed, and as Christ blessed the wedding at Cana.
The order of the service, step by step

The West Syriac order of marriage has two parts, which today are usually celebrated together in the church, before or connected with the Holy Qurbono. The exact texts follow the approved order (Taksa) of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church.

1. The betrothal and the blessing of the rings. After the opening prayers, psalms and the Promiun and Sedro with incense, the priest asks the bride and bridegroom for their free consent before the Church. He blesses the rings, which are placed on their fingers as a pledge of faithfulness.
2. The Word of God. Readings from the Apostle (often Ephesians 5) and from the Gospel (often the wedding at Cana, or Matthew 19 on the indissolubility of marriage) are proclaimed.

3. The crowning. The priest prays over the crowns and blesses the heads of the bride and bridegroom, crowning them in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Where crowns are not physically placed, as in much Kerala practice, the blessing of the heads with the sign of the cross expresses the same mystery.

4. The minnu and the manthrakodi. The priest blesses the minnu (thali), and the bridegroom ties it around the bride's neck; then he places the manthrakodi, the blessed wedding cloth, upon her head. The priest joins their right hands.
5. Conclusion. The final prayers ask that the couple may live in peace, see their children's children, and come together to the heavenly bridal chamber; the priest blesses them with the cross.
The signs explained

The crown. In the Syriac tradition the couple are crowned as king and queen of a new household, a small kingdom where Christ reigns; as victors over selfishness; and as martyrs, for married love means laying down one's life for the other each day. The Psalm says of the human being: “crowned them with glory and honor” (Psalm 8:5), and Christ promises: “Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10).

The minnu. This small pendant, a sign of marriage from the ancient customs of Kerala, carries for Christians the sign of the cross, often formed of small beads; in many families it is tied with threads drawn from the manthrakodi. It says that the bride is bound to her husband in Christ, and he to her.

The manthrakodi. A new garment, blessed and given by the bridegroom, recalls the white garment of Baptism and the new life the couple begin together. The rings speak of faithfulness without end, and the joined right hands of two lives now held together by God.
Preparation

Marriage is prepared long before the wedding: by a chaste friendship, by prayer and by honest conversation about faith, children, money, work and the two families. The Church requires couples to attend a marriage preparation course and to meet the parish priest in good time; the banns are announced in the parishes so that any impediment can be made known.

The couple should bring the necessary documents (baptismal certificates, the certificate of the preparation course, any permission needed), go to Confession before the wedding and receive Holy Communion, so that they begin their married life in grace (CCC 1622). By long custom, weddings are not celebrated during the Great Fast and certain other fasting seasons; ask the parish priest about the dates.
Marriages across Churches

In Kerala, many Syro-Malankara Catholics marry members of the Syro-Malabar or Latin Catholic Churches, or members of the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Churches, with whom we share the same West Syriac heritage. Such marriages are to be prepared with special care and with the permission required by law, so that both partners respect each other's faith and the children are not torn between two families.

Between Catholics of different Churches sui iuris no special permission is needed, but the law of ascription must be followed; a wife may choose to transfer to her husband's Church, and children are normally ascribed to the Church of their father (CCEO cc. 29, 33). Speak with the parish priest early to know what applies.
Living the sacrament

The grace of the sacrament remains every day: it gives the spouses strength to love, to forgive, to bear one another's burdens and to raise their children in the faith. A family that prays the evening prayer together, takes part in the Holy Qurbono together and forgives each other becomes a domestic church (CCC 1656–1658).

When difficulties come, seek help early: from a priest, a trusted counselor or an experienced couple in the parish. Christ who was present at Cana, and who changed water into wine when the wine ran out, is present in every Christian marriage.
notes: Catholics of an Eastern Church must marry with the sacred rite: before the local hierarch, the parish priest, or a priest given the faculty of blessing the marriage, and in the presence of two witnesses; otherwise the marriage is invalid unless a dispensation has been granted (CCEO c. 828).

Marriage with a baptized non-Catholic requires the permission of the competent authority; marriage with a non-baptized person requires a dispensation. The Catholic party promises to remain faithful and to do all in his or her power to have the children baptized and raised in the Catholic Church (CCEO cc. 813–814; CCC 1633–1637).

When a Catholic of an Eastern Church marries a member of an Eastern non-Catholic Church (for example Malankara Orthodox or Jacobite), the canonical form is required for lawfulness, while for validity the blessing of a priest is required (CCEO c. 834 §2). Never arrange such a marriage without first speaking to the parish priest.
Civil divorce does not dissolve a valid sacramental marriage. Where there is serious doubt about validity, the Church's tribunal can examine the case and, if nullity is proven, declare it (CCC 1629).

Marriage between close relatives is forbidden: in the collateral line it is invalid up to the fourth degree (first cousins) unless a dispensation is given, and some degrees can never be dispensed (CCEO c. 808).
Dowry, its demand and extravagant display contradict the dignity of the sacrament and burden the poor; the Church in India has repeatedly asked the faithful to reject them.

sub: Bishops, priests, deacons and the minor orders in the West Syriac tradition of the Syro-Malankara Church
sec: The priesthood of Christ

Christ is the one High Priest, who offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:26–27). All the baptized share in his priesthood: they offer their lives as a spiritual sacrifice (1 Peter 2:9; CCC 1546). But Christ also chose the Twelve and gave them a special share in his mission: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19); “As the Father has sent me, so I send you” (John 20:21).

Through the sacrament of Holy Orders this mission continues in the Church until the end of time. Those ordained act in the person of Christ the Head, to teach, to sanctify and to shepherd his people (CCC 1548–1551). No one takes this honor upon himself: “one does not presume to take this honor, but takes it only when called by God, just as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5:4).
Three degrees
The bishop receives the fullness of the sacrament. He is a successor of the apostles, the visible sign of unity in the local Church, in communion with the Pope and the other bishops (CCC 1555–1561).

The priest is a co-worker of the bishop: he celebrates the Holy Qurbono, forgives sins, anoints the sick, preaches the Word and cares for the people entrusted to him (CCC 1562–1568). The deacon is ordained for service: he proclaims the Gospel, assists at the altar, leads the people's responses and prayers, and serves the poor (CCC 1569–1571; Acts 6:1–6).
The essential rite

In every rite the essential sign is the laying on of hands by the bishop, with the consecratory prayer asking God to pour out the Holy Spirit for the ministry (CCC 1573). The apostles “prayed and laid their hands on them” (Acts 6:6), and Paul reminds Timothy “to rekindle the gift of God that is within you through the laying on of my hands” (2 Timothy 1:6).

Like Baptism and Chrismation, Holy Orders marks the soul with an indelible character; it cannot be repeated or taken away (CCC 1581–1583). Only a baptized man can validly receive sacred ordination; the Church holds herself bound by the choice made by the Lord himself (CCC 1577). No one has a right to ordination; it is a call from God, discerned and confirmed by the Church (CCC 1578).
The ladder of orders in our Church

The West Syriac tradition keeps a ladder of ministries. The minor orders are the singer (Mzamrono) and the reader (Korooyo), and then the subdeacon (Heupadiyakno). The major orders are the deacon (Shamshono, in Malayalam usage shemmassan), the priest (Kassisso, the achen of our parishes) and the bishop (Episcopo). Seminarians receive the minor orders step by step during their formation, so that they learn to serve the liturgy from below.

Some honorary titles are also given within the order of priests: a senior priest may be named Cor-episcopa, and a monk-priest is called Ramban. These titles honor a service; they are not further degrees of the sacrament.
How a priest is ordained, step by step

Ordinations take place within the Holy Qurbono, celebrated by the bishop. The order below is a simplified description; the exact rite follows the approved Pontifical of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church.
1. Presentation. The candidate, already a deacon, is presented to the bishop, and the Church testifies that he is worthy. Prayers and hymns ask God to choose and strengthen his servant.

2. The laying on of hands. In a striking West Syriac custom, the bishop first holds his hands over the consecrated Holy Mysteries on the altar, as if to receive from Christ the grace he is about to give, and then lays them on the head of the candidate, who kneels before the altar. He prays the consecratory prayer, asking the Holy Spirit to make him a priest.
3. The proclamation. The bishop proclaims publicly that the servant of God N. is called from the order of deacons to the order of priests in the holy Church of God.

4. Vesting and first service. The new priest is vested in the priestly stole and phayno, receives the signs of his ministry, and for the first time takes part at the altar as a priest. The people rejoice and greet him. Soon after, he celebrates his first Holy Qurbono, the puthen Qurbono, usually in his home parish.
Bishops and the Holy Synod

Bishops in the Syriac tradition are chosen from celibate priests, often monks; before episcopal ordination the candidate is usually made a Ramban. He receives the title Mar and a new name, often in the ancient Greek or Syriac form, as Mar Ivanios, Mar Theophilos or Mar Severios. A bishop is ordained by the Major Archbishop-Catholicos or another bishop, with at least two other bishops.

The Syro-Malankara Catholic Church is a Major Archiepiscopal Church sui iuris. Its bishops form the Holy Episcopal Synod, presided over by the Major Archbishop-Catholicos. Within the Church's own territory the Synod elects bishops, with the assent of the Pope; outside that territory the Pope appoints them. The Major Archbishop is elected by the Synod and confirmed by the Pope (CCEO cc. 151–154, 181–182).
Priests in the life of our Church

The priest is the father of the parish: he offers the Holy Qurbono, baptizes, hears confessions, anoints the sick, blesses homes and marriages, buries the dead, teaches the faith and visits the families. Priests of the Syro-Malankara Church are formed in its seminaries, especially St Mary's Malankara Major Seminary in Thiruvananthapuram, and in the houses of religious communities such as the Order of the Imitation of Christ (Bethany), founded by Mar Ivanios.

Since the Reunion of 1930, the diocesan clergy of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church have in practice been celibate; the older West Syriac tradition, still kept by the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Churches, also knows married priests. This is a matter of each Church's discipline, not of faith; follow the particular law of our Church.
Praying for vocations and for our priests

“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37–38). Every family can pray for vocations and encourage a son or daughter who feels the call to the priesthood or religious life.

Pray for your priests and bishops every day. Respect them, help them, and correct with charity when needed. A priest is “chosen from among mortals” and “put in charge of things pertaining to God on their behalf” (Hebrews 5:1); he needs the prayer and friendship of his community.
notes: Only a bishop can validly ordain (CCC 1576). In our Church the ordination of bishops follows the canonical provision of the Holy Episcopal Synod in communion with the Pope (CCEO cc. 181–182); ordination without lawful provision is gravely forbidden.

Candidates are formed for many years in seminaries and must be freely chosen, mature, and of sound faith and morals; the Church examines their suitability with care, and no family may pressure a son into ordination.

Celibacy and married clergy are governed by the particular law of each Church sui iuris (CCEO c. 373); the practice described above should be checked against the current norms of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church.

A priest who leaves the ministry remains a priest by the character received; he may be dispensed from the obligations of the clerical state only by the competent authority of the Holy See or, within its limits, of the Church sui iuris.

Any abuse of minors or vulnerable adults by a cleric must be reported to the bishop and, where the law requires, to the civil authorities; the Church has strict norms for this (Vos estis lux mundi, 2019, 2023).
The faithful may not treat priests as servants of family prestige; offerings for the Holy Qurbono are a gift for the support of the clergy, never a price for the sacrament.

sub: The Shehimo: the seven hours of the West Syriac day, prayed by the Syro-Malankara Church
sec: Praying without ceasing

“Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). From the beginning the Church prayed at fixed hours, as Israel did: “Seven times a day I praise you” (Psalm 119:164); “Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he will hear my voice” (Psalm 55:17). Peter went up on the roof to pray about noon, and Peter and John went to the temple “at the hour of prayer, at three o'clock in the afternoon” (Acts 10:9; 3:1).

The Prayer of the Hours sanctifies the whole day and night: it extends to every hour the praise and thanksgiving of the Holy Qurbono (CCC 1174–1178). It is the prayer of Christ with his Body, the Church, to the Father. When we pray it, even alone at home, we pray with the whole Church and in her name.
The day begins in the evening

In the Syriac tradition, as in the Bible, the liturgical day begins at sunset: “And there was evening and there was morning, the first day” (Genesis 1:5). So the Sunday begins on Saturday evening, and every feast begins with its evening prayer.

The West Syriac Church keeps seven hours of prayer: Ramsho (evening prayer), Soothoro (the prayer before sleep), Lilyo (the night prayer, with its watches), Sapro (morning prayer), and the third, sixth and ninth hours of the day (Tloth sho'in, Sheth sho'in and Tsha' sho'in). In parish and family practice they are often grouped: the evening and the prayer before sleep together in the evening; the night, morning and third hours together in the morning; the sixth at midday and the ninth in the afternoon.
The hours and the mystery of Christ

Each hour is a window onto the saving work of Christ. Evening recalls the evening sacrifice and the Lord's burial and rest; the prayer before sleep entrusts our sleep, the image of death, to God; the night watch waits for the Bridegroom who comes at midnight (Matthew 25:6); the morning greets the risen Christ, the true Light. The third hour recalls the condemnation of the Lord and the descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:15); the sixth his crucifixion; the ninth his death on the Cross.
So the day becomes a path through the Passion and Resurrection. The Church does not pray the hours to fill time, but to let Christ's Pasch shape every part of our day.
The shape of an hour, step by step
The hours of the Shehimo follow a recognizable pattern. The exact texts are in the approved books of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church.
1. Opening. The prayer begins with the glory to the Holy Trinity and, when a priest leads, his blessing, to which the people answer “Amen”.

2. The Kauma. This short series of prayers begins every hour: the Trisagion, sung three times (“Holy are you, O God; holy are you, Almighty; holy are you, Immortal; crucified for us, have mercy on us”), “Kurielaison”, and the Lord's Prayer. Its words, addressed to Christ crucified, are a summary of our faith.

3. The Psalms. Psalm 51 (the Miserere) is said at most hours. At Ramsho the evening psalms are sung, among them Psalm 141: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you, and the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 141:2). At Sapro come the morning psalms, such as Psalm 63 and the psalms of praise (Psalms 148–150).

4. Hymns and prayers. In the fuller form the Promiun and Sedro are prayed with incense; then come the hymns (qole), many by St Ephrem and St Jacob of Serugh, and the Bo'utho, rhythmic supplications in the metres of St Ephrem, St Jacob and St Balai. The hymns follow a set order of themes: the Mother of God, the saints, the departed, repentance and the Cross.
5. Conclusion. The hour ends with the Kauma again and the Lord's Prayer; in some hours the Nicene Creed is professed. Then all bow for the blessing.
The books: Shehimo and Fenqitho

The Shehimo (from a Syriac word meaning “simple” or “ordinary”) is the book of the weekday hours, with a set of prayers for each day of the week. It is short enough to be used by priests, religious and many lay families. On Sundays and great feasts the Church sings the richer festal hours, gathered in the volumes called the Fenqitho.

These prayers are a school of theology. Their hymns teach the Incarnation, the virginity and divine motherhood of Mary, the power of the Cross, the resurrection of the dead and the mercy of God, in the poetic language of the Syriac Fathers. The Kurisumala Ashram at Vagamon, a Cistercian monastery of the Syro-Malankara Church, prepared a celebrated English translation of the West Syriac Hours, Prayer with the Harp of the Spirit.
Gestures and posture

The Syriac tradition prays the hours standing and facing east, the direction of the rising sun and of Christ who will come again. The faithful make the sign of the cross at the Trisagion and at the glory to the Trinity, and bow at the blessing. When a priest or deacon leads, incense rises like prayer.

In the Great Fast the hours are accompanied by prostrations: at certain prayers the faithful kneel and touch the ground with their foreheads, a bodily act of repentance and adoration. The hymns are sung in the eight tones of the West Syriac tradition, which change from week to week; even a family that cannot sing them well should try to pray them aloud and together.
The Shehimo at home

The evening prayer is the oldest family prayer of the Thomas Christians. At sunset the lamp is lit, the family gathers before the cross, and the evening prayer is said, followed by the prayer before sleep. Many Syro-Malankara families pray the Shehimo in Malayalam in this way every day; children learn its responses by heart long before they can read.

If the full hour is too long for your family, begin with the Kauma, a psalm, one hymn and the Lord's Prayer, and grow little by little. A family that prays the Church's own prayer every evening is formed by it for life.
Praying with the whole Church

Priests, deacons and religious pray the Hours daily on behalf of the whole Church; when lay people pray with them, the small prayer of a home joins the great prayer of the Church. The Second Vatican Council asked pastors to see that the principal hours are celebrated in common in church on Sundays and feasts, and encouraged lay people to pray them with the priests, among themselves or individually (Sacrosanctum Concilium 100).
Where the parish celebrates Ramsho on Saturday evening or before a feast, take part in it. It prepares the heart for the Holy Qurbono of the next day.
notes: Clerics are bound to pray the Divine Office daily according to the particular law of their own Church sui iuris (CCEO c. 377); deacons and religious follow the norms laid down for them.
The Prayer of the Hours is the public prayer of the Church; private devotions are good, but they should lead to the liturgy and never replace it (Sacrosanctum Concilium 13).
Use the approved books of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church; do not mix texts from other traditions into the liturgical hours on your own initiative.
The prostrations of the Great Fast may be adapted for the elderly, the sick and pregnant women; a deep bow or the sign of the cross expresses the same repentance.
Do not rush the prayer to finish it; it is better to pray one hour attentively than several mechanically (Matthew 6:7).
The Shehimo shares many texts with the prayers of the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Churches; this common heritage is a gift that unites the Christians of Kerala in prayer.

sub: Holy water, the cross, the blessings of the year and popular piety in the West Syriac tradition of the Syro-Malankara Church
sec: What sacramentals are

Sacramentals are sacred signs instituted by the Church, which resemble the sacraments: they signify spiritual effects obtained through the prayer of the Church. They dispose us to receive the grace of the sacraments and sanctify the various circumstances of life (CCC 1667–1670).

Among them, blessings come first: blessings of persons, of homes and work, of meals, of objects used in prayer. Others are holy water, blessed candles and palms, the cross, medals, the rosary, and the consecration of churches and altars. St Paul gives the principle: “everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected, provided it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by God's word and by prayer” (1 Timothy 4:4–5).
Not magic, but faith

A sacramental does not work by itself like a charm. Its power comes from the prayer of the Church and from the faith and love with which it is used (CCC 1670). Holy water on the forehead recalls our Baptism; a blessed cross in the home declares that Christ is its Lord; a blessed palm reminds us that we welcomed Christ as King.

Superstition gives to signs a power they do not have; it is a sin against the first commandment (CCC 2111). Fortune-telling, horoscopes, charms against the evil eye, consulting the stars for wedding dates and the like are contrary to faith and must be avoided (CCC 2116–2117).
The cross in our tradition

The Thomas Christians of Kerala have from ancient times honored the cross, often without the figure of the Crucified, as the sign of Christ's victory and of the Resurrection: the cross of light that will appear when the Son of Man comes. In Syro-Malankara churches the cross stands on the altar, and the priest blesses with a hand cross, often covered with a small veil; the faithful kiss it with reverence when they greet the priest.

The Church celebrates the Feast of the Holy Cross (Sleebo) on 14 September. In the middle of the Great Fast a cross is set up and honored in the church, encouraging the faithful to complete the fast, and on Good Friday the cross is venerated and laid to rest. Many families keep a cross in the place of prayer and make its sign on their children every night.
Blessings through the year, step by step
1. Denho (Theophany, 6 January). The water is blessed in memory of the Lord's Baptism in the Jordan; the faithful take it home, drink it with prayer, and sprinkle their homes and fields.
2. Shubkono (the beginning of the Great Fast). At the service of reconciliation the faithful ask forgiveness of one another, often with prostrations, before entering the fast.
3. Hosanna (Palm Sunday). Palms or tender coconut leaves (kuruthola) are blessed and carried in procession with the cry “Hosanna”; the blessed leaves are kept reverently at home.

4. Pesaha and Good Friday. On Thursday the Lord's washing of the feet is enacted; in many families the Pesaha bread is broken at home in memory of the Last Supper. On Good Friday the faithful venerate the cross, and in many places they taste the bitter drink (kaippuneer), remembering the vinegar given to the Lord.
5. Qyomtho (Easter). The joy of the Resurrection is proclaimed, and the faithful exchange the peace and greet one another with the Easter greeting.

6. The feast of the parish. The feast of the patron saint is celebrated with the Holy Qurbono, a procession with the cross and decorated umbrellas, and the blessing of the people and of their offerings.
Blessings of home and life

The priest blesses a new house with prayers, incense and holy water; he goes from room to room, asking God to keep the family in peace, health and faith. Many families also ask him to bless the foundation stone of a house, a new shop or vehicle, the first fruits of the harvest, and the family when it gathers for an important event.

Parents bless their children with the sign of the cross on the forehead before sleep and before a journey or an examination; it is a beautiful gesture of the baptized. The ancient blessing of Israel can be used at home: “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you, and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you, and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24–26).
Holy places, relics and saints

The faithful honor the relics and the tombs of the saints as places of prayer, since the bodies of the saints were temples of the Holy Spirit. The tomb of Mar Ivanios at St Mary's Cathedral, Pattom, Thiruvananthapuram, is a place of pilgrimage; many come to pray there, especially around the anniversary of his death on 15 July.

Our people love the Mother of God. The fast before the feast of her Nativity (the eight days from 1 to 8 September) is kept with great devotion in many churches, and Marian prayers are part of every hour of the Shehimo. The Syriac tradition also honors the saints of the whole Church, from the apostles and martyrs to the Syriac Fathers Ephrem and Jacob of Serugh.
Popular piety

The faith of our people is expressed in many devotions: processions, novenas, pilgrimages, the lighting of lamps and candles, the rosary, the Way of the Cross, and vows and offerings (nercha) at churches and shrines. The Church values this popular piety and guides it so that it leads to Christ and to the liturgy (CCC 1674–1676).

Some of these devotions, such as the rosary and the Way of the Cross, came to us from the Latin Church; they are good and approved. They should be practiced in harmony with the liturgical year and should never take the place of the Holy Qurbono or of the hours of our own tradition.
Blessings in daily life

Keep holy water at home and use it with a prayer, especially at night and in times of fear or sickness. Before and after meals, at the beginning of a journey, before work or study, a short blessing and the sign of the cross turn ordinary life into prayer.

Ask the priest to visit and bless your home at least once a year. Teach children the meaning of each sign, so that the cross, the lamp, the holy water and the blessed palm speak to them of Christ and not of luck.
notes: Blessed objects should be treated with reverence; when worn out, they are burned or buried, not thrown away with rubbish.

Exorcism in the strict sense may be performed only by a priest with the express permission of the bishop (CCC 1673). Those troubled should first be seen by a priest and, where needed, by a doctor; many troubles have natural causes.
Do not buy or sell blessed objects for their blessing; the price is only for the material.
Some blessings are reserved to bishops or priests; others may be given by lay people, especially by parents for their children (CCC 1669).

Vows and offerings (nercha) are good when they come from faith and gratitude, never when they become a bargain with God or a substitute for conversion; fulfil what you promised, and ask a priest if a vow becomes impossible to keep.
Popular devotions must follow the guidance of the Church; new devotions, messages or apparitions are not to be promoted in churches without the approval of the bishop.

sub: The West Syriac burial services: how the Syro-Malankara Church accompanies the dead and comforts the living
sec: Christian hope before death

“I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live” (John 11:25). For Christians death is not the end but a passage: life is changed, not ended (CCC 1012). The body that was the temple of the Holy Spirit will rise again on the last day.

St Paul writes so that we “may not grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Therefore the Church accompanies her children to the end with prayer, honors their bodies with reverence, and continues to pray for them after death (CCC 1680–1684).
Praying for the dead

Scripture already praises prayer for the dead, that they might be delivered from their sin (2 Maccabees 12:43–46). Those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully purified undergo purification after death, which the Church calls purgatory (CCC 1030–1032).

Our prayers, especially the Holy Qurbono offered for them, almsgiving and works of penance, help the departed. In every Holy Qurbono the Church remembers the faithful departed in the great intercessions (Thubden). The communion of saints unites the living and the dead in one family of God.
Different services for different lives

The West Syriac tradition has distinct burial services for bishops and priests, for deacons, for laymen, for laywomen and for children. Each speaks of the life the person lived: the priest who served at the altar, the mother who gave life, the child who goes straight to God.

The service for little children who die after Baptism is different in tone: it is less a prayer for forgiveness than a hymn of trust, because the Church believes that baptized children who die before the age of reason enter the Kingdom of God. Their parents are comforted with the image of the Lord who said, “Let the little children come to me” (Mark 10:14).
The service, step by step

The burial service is sung in several parts, following the approved order (Taksa) of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church. Customs differ somewhat from place to place; the outline below is the common pattern.

1. At the home. When death comes, the family prays, closes the eyes of the departed, washes and clothes the body, places a cross in the hands and lights a lamp near the head. The priest comes and the first part of the service is sung, with the Kauma, psalms, hymns of hope and incense. Relatives and neighbors keep watch and pray.

2. The procession to the church. The body is carried to the church with the cross, candles and hymns. In the church it is placed in the nave facing east, toward the altar; by ancient custom the body of a priest is placed facing the people, as he faced them in life when he blessed them.

3. In the church. The main parts of the service are sung, each with its Promiun and Sedro with incense, readings from the Apostle (such as 1 Thessalonians 4 or 1 Corinthians 15) and the Gospel (such as John 5 or John 11), and the hymns of St Ephrem, which speak of the earth as a womb that will give back the dead on the day of the resurrection.

4. The farewell. In a moving part of the service the hymns give voice to the departed, who bids farewell to the church, to the altar where he received the Holy Mysteries, to his family and friends. The faithful come forward to give the last kiss, usually to the cross held over the body.

5. At the grave. The priest blesses the grave, casts earth upon the body in the form of a cross, recalling the word spoken to Adam: “you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19), and incenses it; the last prayers commend the departed to Christ, the Lord of the living and the dead.
Bishops and priests

The burial service of a priest is the longest and most solemn. The body is vested in the liturgical vestments, as one who stands ready to serve at the altar of heaven, and the Gospel book is often placed near him. In the Syriac tradition bishops are laid to rest with special honor and long prayers, surrounded by the clergy and the faithful.
These customs teach the whole Church that the priesthood is a service unto death, and that the shepherd who offered the Holy Qurbono for his people now needs their prayers in return.
Remembering the departed

According to custom the departed are remembered with the Holy Qurbono and prayers at the grave on the third day, the ninth day, the thirtieth or fortieth day and on the anniversary; the days observed vary somewhat between places and families. The memorial meal that follows should be simple, an act of fellowship and charity, not of display.

The Church's great days of remembrance are the Sunday of the Departed Priests (Kohne) and the Sunday of All the Faithful Departed (Aneede), just before the Great Fast. Many families also visit the graves, light candles and pray there on these days and on the anniversaries of their dead.
Grief and consolation

Jesus wept at the tomb of his friend Lazarus (John 11:35). Christian faith does not forbid tears; it gives them hope. Families should be allowed to grieve, and the parish community should surround them with prayer, presence and practical help.

Visit the bereaved after the funeral, not only on the day. Remember the dead by name at family prayer and on anniversaries. Teach children that we will see our loved ones again in Christ, and that love does not end with death.
When death is hard

Some deaths are especially painful: the death of a child, a sudden accident, a long illness, or a suicide. The Church does not judge the departed but entrusts them to the mercy of God, who alone sees the heart; she prays for them and comforts their families (CCC 2283).

Priests and parish communities should show special compassion in such cases, helping the family with the arrangements, offering the Holy Qurbono for the departed, and staying close in the months that follow, when grief is often deepest.
notes: The Church earnestly recommends burial of the body; cremation is permitted when it is not chosen for reasons contrary to Christian faith. The ashes must be kept in a sacred place (cemetery or church), not scattered, divided or kept at home (Ad resurgendum cum Christo, 2016).

Ecclesiastical funeral rites are not denied to Catholics except in the cases foreseen by law, such as notorious apostasy or other grave public scandal without any sign of repentance before death; when in doubt, the bishop decides (CCEO cc. 875–878).
Pastors should show special compassion to families after tragic deaths, including suicide, for which the Church prays and hopes in God's mercy (CCC 2283).

Baptized members of other Churches, such as the Malankara Orthodox or Jacobite Churches, may in certain cases be given Catholic funeral rites when their own minister is not available and it is not against their wishes (c. 1183 §3; cf. CCEO c. 876).
Organ donation after death is a noble and meritorious act, to be encouraged as an expression of generous solidarity, provided death has been certified properly (CCC 2296).
Lavish display at funerals and feasts that burden the family is contrary to Christian simplicity; offer the Holy Qurbono and alms for the departed instead.
