t: The Story of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church
sub: From the Apostle Thomas to the Reunion of 1930 and the Major Archiepiscopal Church of today
sec: The Apostle Thomas and the Church of India

The Christians of Kerala trace their faith to St Thomas the Apostle, who, according to an ancient and living tradition, landed at Kodungallur (Muziris) in AD 52, preached the Gospel along the Malabar coast, founded communities and was martyred near Mylapore (Chennai). This is why they are called the St Thomas Christians or Nasranis. The tradition is very old and was received by the wider Church; the details of the Apostle's journeys cannot be proved by documents, but the faith of a Church that has lived for many centuries is itself a witness.

For more than fifteen centuries the St Thomas Christians formed one Church, with one apostolic heritage. The Syro-Malankara Catholic Church is one of the heirs of this single family, together with the Syro-Malabar Church and the other Churches of the Thomas Christian tradition.
Centuries of communion with the East

From early times the Thomas Christians received bishops from the Church of the East in Persia and Mesopotamia, and they celebrated the liturgy in Syriac according to the East Syriac tradition. The bishops were usually foreigners who ordained and taught; the daily government of the community was in the hands of a native leader, the Archdeacon (Jathikku Karthavyan), and of the assemblies (yogam) of the parishes.

The community had its own way of life, the “Law of Thomas”: Christian in faith and worship, Indian in culture, dress and custom, and respected by the Hindu rulers of Kerala. Its churches, crosses and customs were a sign that the Gospel had taken root in Indian soil long before the arrival of Europeans.
The Portuguese and the Synod of Diamper

When the Portuguese came at the end of the fifteenth century, they met the Thomas Christians with joy, as fellow Christians. But misunderstandings grew: the missionaries did not know the Syriac tradition, and they suspected its books and customs. In 1599 Archbishop Alexis de Menezes of Goa convened the Synod of Diamper (Udayamperur), which placed the community under Latin bishops, burned or corrected many Syriac books and introduced Latin customs.

The Catholic Church today recognizes that much of the Thomas Christian heritage was then wounded, and it has asked the Eastern Churches to restore their authentic traditions (Orientalium Ecclesiarum 6; Congregation for the Eastern Churches, Instruction for Applying the Liturgical Prescriptions of the CCEO, 1996). This history is remembered not to accuse, but to understand and to heal.
The Coonan Cross Oath of 1653

Tension grew for half a century. In 1652 a bishop from the East, Ahatallah, arrived in India, was detained by the Portuguese, and rumors spread that he had been put to death. On 3 January 1653 a great number of Thomas Christians gathered at Mattancherry, near Kochi, and, holding a rope tied to a cross that was too small for all to touch, swore that they would no longer obey the Jesuit prelate imposed on them. The cross is remembered as the Coonan (bent) Cross.

The oath was a protest against foreign domination, not a rejection of the Catholic faith. Soon afterwards the Archdeacon Thomas was raised to the rank of bishop by the laying on of hands of twelve priests and became Mar Thoma I. Rome sent Carmelite missionaries, and through their efforts a large part of the community returned to communion with the Pope; they became known as the Pazhayakoor (old party). Those who remained with Mar Thoma came to be called the Puthenkoor (new party). One family was now divided in two.
The Antiochene connection

In 1665 Mar Gregorios Abdul Jaleel, a bishop of the Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch from Jerusalem, came to Kerala and was received by Mar Thoma I. From then on the Puthenkoor community was linked with the Syriac Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch, and over the following centuries it gradually adopted the West Syriac (Antiochene) liturgy, with the Anaphora of St James, the Shehimo and the rich hymns of the Syriac Fathers.

Through these centuries there were repeated longings for reunion with Rome; around 1799 Mar Thoma VI (Mar Dionysius I) entered Catholic communion for a short time. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the Malankara Church passed through further divisions: a reform movement gave rise to the Mar Thoma Syrian Church, and disputes over the authority of the Patriarch of Antioch and of the Catholicos established in Kerala in 1912 separated what are today the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church and the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church. Catholics speak of these sister Churches with respect: their sorrows are also ours.
Mar Ivanios and Bethany

Geevarghese Panickerveetil was born at Mavelikara on 21 September 1882. A brilliant student, he took a master's degree at Madras Christian College, was ordained a priest in 1908, and taught at the seminary in Kottayam and later at Serampore College in Bengal. There he dreamed of a religious life that would unite the monastic heritage of the East with the spirit of India.

In 1919 he founded the Bethany Ashram at Mundanmala near Ranni-Perunad, the Order of the Imitation of Christ, and in 1925 a congregation of sisters, the Bethany Madhom. In 1925 he was consecrated bishop with the name Mar Ivanios. Prayer, study of the Fathers and the history of the Church led him to a deep conviction: the Church founded by Christ on Peter must be one, and the Malankara Church should return to the communion it had once enjoyed with the See of Rome.
The Reunion of 20 September 1930

In 1926 the bishops of the Malankara Church authorized Mar Ivanios to open discussions with Rome about reunion. The Holy See asked only for the Catholic faith and communion with the Pope; it promised that the West Syriac liturgy would be preserved whole, and that bishops whose baptism and ordination were valid would keep their episcopal dignity.

On 20 September 1930, at Kollam, Mar Ivanios and Mar Theophilos, with a small group of companions, made their profession of the Catholic faith before Bishop Aloysius Maria Benziger of Quilon. This is the Reunion (Punaraikyam) that the Church celebrates every year. On 11 June 1932 Pope Pius XI established the hierarchy by the bull Christo Pastorum Principi: the Archeparchy of Trivandrum with Mar Ivanios as Archbishop, and the Eparchy of Tiruvalla with Mar Theophilos as bishop. Other bishops, priests and many lay people followed, among them Joseph Mar Severios in 1937.

Mar Ivanios died on 15 July 1953 and was laid to rest in St Mary's Cathedral, Pattom, Thiruvananthapuram. The cause for his beatification has been opened, and the faithful honor him as Servant of God.
Growth after the Reunion

Under Archbishop Benedict Mar Gregorios (1955–1994) and Archbishop Cyril Mar Baselios (1995–2007) the young Church grew in parishes, schools, colleges, hospitals and works of charity, among them Mar Ivanios College in Thiruvananthapuram. Its mission reached the poor and the marginalized in southern Kerala and Kanyakumari, the migrant settlers of Malabar, and the faithful in the cities of India and abroad.

Monastic life flourished alongside Bethany: in 1958 the Kurisumala Ashram at Vagamon was founded in the Syro-Malankara rite by Fr Francis Mahieu (Francis Acharya), with the participation of Fr Bede Griffiths, uniting Cistercian life with the Syriac liturgy and Indian simplicity. The liturgy was celebrated in Malayalam, and the Church worked steadily to keep its West Syriac heritage pure and living.
A Major Archiepiscopal Church today

On 10 February 2005 Pope John Paul II raised the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church to the rank of a Major Archiepiscopal Church, and Cyril Mar Baselios became its first Major Archbishop; the Church's Synod gave him the traditional title of Catholicos. After his death in 2007 the Holy Episcopal Synod elected Baselios Mar Cleemis, whom Pope Benedict XVI created a Cardinal in 2012. The Church is a Church sui iuris governed by its Major Archbishop-Catholicos and Synod, in full communion with the Pope (CCEO cc. 151–154).

Its jurisdictions include the Major Archeparchy of Trivandrum and the Archeparchy of Tiruvalla, with eparchies such as Bathery, Marthandom, Muvattupuzha, Mavelikara, Pathanamthitta, Parassala, Puthur, Gurugram, Khadki (Pune), and an eparchy for the United States and Canada, together with pastoral care for the faithful in the Gulf, Europe and Oceania. The number and boundaries of these jurisdictions may change; consult the Church's official directory for the current list.
Sister Churches and the hope of unity

The Syro-Malankara Catholic Church shares its liturgy, its hymns, its saints and much of its history with the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church and the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church. Catholics recognize that these Churches have true sacraments, above all the priesthood and the Eucharist (Unitatis Redintegratio 15). Since 1984, when Pope John Paul II and Patriarch Ignatius Zakka I signed a common declaration, and since the dialogue begun with the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church in 1989, these Churches have grown in mutual understanding.

Mar Ivanios understood the Reunion not as a victory over anyone, but as a step toward the unity for which Christ prayed: “that they may all be one” (John 17:21). Our Church is called to be a bridge: faithful to the Catholic communion, faithful to the Syriac heritage, and patient and loving toward our brothers and sisters in the other Malankara Churches, with whom we share families, villages and a common faith in Christ.
notes: The Syro-Malankara Catholic Church is a Church sui iuris of equal dignity with the other Catholic Churches; its members remain members of it wherever they live, and changes of Church follow the norms of law (Orientalium Ecclesiarum 3; CCEO cc. 29–38).
The tradition of St Thomas's coming to India is ancient and venerable, but many details (exact places and dates) are not documented; teach it as the Church's tradition, without exaggeration.

Speak of the Malankara Orthodox, Jacobite, Mar Thoma and other Churches with respect; avoid polemical words and do not take sides in their internal disputes or court cases. Proselytism by pressure or inducement is contrary to the Gospel and to ecumenism.
The Reunion Day (20 September) is a day of thanksgiving and of prayer for Christian unity, not of triumph over others.
Mar Ivanios is honored as Servant of God; public liturgical veneration as Blessed or Saint must await the judgment of the Church, though private prayer for his intercession is encouraged.
